C++.justification: `int32_t v; if(cond){v=5;}else{v=9;} return v;` — C++ permits declaration without initializer; definite assignment on both branches makes subsequent read well-defined.

Go.justification: var v int32 declared without initializer, definite assignment on both branches, then read/returned. Go zero-initializes v but that affects determinacy/hidden-cost metrics only, not support (support criteria are behavior-delivery only).

Java.justification: Java definite-assignment analysis permits declare-without-initializer then assign on both branches of an if/else, exactly the pattern required.

Kotlin.justification: Kotlin performs definite-assignment analysis: `val v: Int` (or var) declared without initializer, assigned on both branches of an if/else, then read is accepted by the compiler.

Python.justification: Python requires no separate declaration step; v is definitely assigned on both branches and readable after, satisfying all numbered sub-requirements under the frozen recipe.

Quidra.citation: language.md 'Bindings and definite initialization' example is verbatim this probe: `int x; if true x=1 else x=2; print(x)`.

Quidra.justification: language.md 'Bindings and definite initialization' example is verbatim this probe: `int x; if true x=1 else x=2; print(x)`.

Swift.justification: var v: Int32; if cond { v = 5 } else { v = 9 }; return v — Swift's definite-initialization analysis accepts this on all-paths-assigned patterns.

TypeScript.justification: let v: number; declared without initializer; TS definite-assignment analysis accepts both-branch assignment before read under --strict.

Zig.justification: var v: i32 = undefined; then definite assignment on both branches of an if; Zig's `undefined` is the documented explicit uninitialized-storage marker satisfying R9's non-placeholder requirement (uninitialized is a first-class concept, not a hidden zero-fill).
